# OpenLimiter

> OpenLimiter is a local first quota meter for AI coding subscriptions. It reads the quota your own machine already knows about, keeps every number bounded, and gives coding agents a budget context block they can act on.

Version 1.2.0. Licence: Apache 2.0. Site: https://openlimiter.com

When you hold several AI coding subscriptions at once, the scarce resource stops being money and becomes quota. You have already paid. The question is which of the windows you paid for still has room in it, and OpenLimiter puts that answer in front of the agent that is spending it, as bounded state rather than prose.

## What it is

OpenLimiter reads quota data that already exists on your disk or is piped to it, normalises it, caches it locally, and exposes it three ways: to a person on a command line or a screen, and to an agent as a structured budget block injected into that agent's own context. The block carries enum codes, bounded percentages and timestamps only, and it declares itself as untrusted data in its own opening tag.

Everything you can see is free. Alerts, history, phone access, extra accounts and spend tracking above 100 US dollars a calendar month for each source are Pro. A free account adds sync between your own devices, on from the moment you sign in, and a paid plan called Pro adds four hosted services and two local switches on top of that.

## What ships today

- Command line tool, published on npm as `openlimiter`. Install it with `npm install -g openlimiter`. Commands include init, snapshot, statusline, hook, hooks, ingest, doctor, demo, export, status and serve.
- Desktop tray application for Windows, macOS and Linux, built on continuous integration and attached to the GitHub release. Windows and macOS ship unsigned. In SmartScreen, choose More info, then Run anyway. macOS ships as one unsigned universal disk image that runs on Apple silicon and on Intel: open the app once, then open System Settings, go to Privacy and Security, and choose Open Anyway. macOS is excluded from automatic updates until signed and notarised builds exist.
- Web app at https://openlimiter.com/app. It runs the same engine inside a browser tab. Signed in, it shows the bounded percentages your own devices synced. A document you paste or drop is parsed in the tab and is never uploaded.
- Progressive web app. The web app installs to a phone or desktop home screen from the browser and keeps working offline. There is no iOS or Android application, nothing is in a store, and there is no waiting list.
- A free account, with sign in through GitHub, Google, or a magic link sent to your email address. Sync is on from the moment you sign in, because moving your own percentages between your own devices is what signing in is for. It syncs bounded quota readings and nothing else.
- Phone access by QR pairing. The desktop application shows a code that lives for two minutes, the phone scans it, the desktop approves it, and the phone then holds a read only token. It can never change the account or upload anything, and revoking the device ends its access at once.
- LAN serving with `openlimiter serve`, which publishes read only quota on your local network behind a token that is generated on every start and never written to disk. It is meant for a trusted home or office network, not for the internet.
- Agent adapters that inject the bounded budget block, installed with `openlimiter hooks install <agent>`.

## Pro

Pro costs 5 US dollars a month or 50 US dollars a year, with the first 30 days free and no card required. OpenLimiter Pro is sold by Lucas Costa. Checkout runs through Stripe, which acts as the payment processor and calculates tax automatically. A full refund is available on request within 14 days of any charge, and cancellation is self service through the Stripe Customer Portal.

Pro is five features. Three are hosted services and two are switches in the local application:

- Every alert: a desktop notification, an email and a phone push at 60, 80 and 90 percent of a window, and when a window resets. Hosted.
- Ninety days of history, with a forecast to the day a window runs out. Hosted.
- API spend meters, shipped as a labelled beta. The free plan tracks up to 100 US dollars a calendar month for each source and Pro goes above it. It needs an organisation admin or management key and a project key will not work. Hosted.
- More than one account per provider, unlocked in the local application. The free plan allows one active account per provider. Local.
- One Pro accent or density preset, applied in the local application. Local.

Moonshot is read as a balance rather than as spend: three separate figures, available, voucher and cash, in the currency the provider states. A balance never becomes a monthly figure, a forecast or a budget alert.

## What it never does

- No telemetry from the application. The desktop app, the command line tool and the web app send nothing.
- The website counts page views without cookies, through Vercel Web Analytics. No profile is built and nothing follows a reader to another site.
- No collection, storage or forwarding of provider credentials or API keys. They stay in your operating system keyring and are sent only to the provider they belong to, never to OpenLimiter.
- No writing to what it reads. Every parser opens what your installed tools already stored, read only, and never rewrites, repairs or migrates them.
- No automatic routing. OpenLimiter produces advice. It does not switch a request, bypass a limit, or touch how an agent authenticates. The decision stays with the person.
- No invented numbers. When a shape changes, parsing fails closed: that provider returns to unknown, the others are unaffected, and unknown never becomes zero. A gap in history stays a gap and is never interpolated.

## Connectors

Nine ship in 1.2.0. Every one is marked UNVERIFIED, which means no explicit verifier has confirmed its shape against a live account. In the command line tool no connector performs network access: each one is a parser, and something else has to hand it a document. The desktop application reads Codex, Gemini CLI, Grok, Kimi and OpenRouter live.

- `claude`: reads the rate limit block of the Claude Code statusline payload. Native payload from a local tool. Low automation risk.
- `openrouter`: reads a credits response shape from OpenRouter's documented API. Documented API. Low automation risk.
- `codex`: reads a usage payload the Codex tooling produces. Internal endpoint. May break without notice.
- `antigravity`: reads a quota payload the Antigravity tooling produces. Internal endpoint. May break without notice.
- `gemini_cli`: reads the quota buckets the Gemini CLI defines for its own models. Internal endpoint. High automation risk.
- `grok`: reads the billing response behind the Grok CLI, with its weekly credit window. Internal endpoint. High automation risk.
- `kimi`: reads the usage response the Kimi CLI defines, with its weekly summary and five hour limit. Internal endpoint. High automation risk.
- `opencode`: reads a usage view behind a session you already signed in to. Authenticated page. High automation risk. May break.
- `manual`: reads numbers you write yourself. Manual entry. Never breaks, never guesses.

## Agent adapters

Support means a live fixture was observed delivering the block on a real machine, not that an adapter exists.

- Claude Code: supported from 2.1.257. `openlimiter hooks install claude`.
- Codex CLI: supported from 0.152.0. `openlimiter hooks install codex`.
- Gemini CLI: adapter built, gated until a fixture passes.
- Kimi Code CLI: adapter built, gated. Version 1.50.0 discards what the hook prints.
- Antigravity CLI: excluded. The installed CLI exposes no hooks subcommand.
- OpenCode: experimental and off by default, pinned to 1.18.11 and requiring `OPENLIMITER_EXPERIMENTAL_OPENCODE=1`.
- Grok Build: not supported for injection, because Grok discards what a successful hook prints. Run `openlimiter status --agent-context` instead.

## Documentation

- [Getting started](https://openlimiter.com/docs): install the tool, run the demo, and wire it into an agent.
- [Why OpenLimiter](https://openlimiter.com/docs/why-openlimiter): the problem it addresses, and why quota rather than cost.
- [Supported providers](https://openlimiter.com/docs/providers): the nine connectors, what each reads, and how likely each is to break.
- [Ingestion](https://openlimiter.com/docs/ingestion): the three offline paths that put quota data in front of the tool.
- [Agent context](https://openlimiter.com/docs/agent-context): what the statusline and the prompt hook inject, which agents receive it, and the boundary that keeps provider text out.
- [Configuration](https://openlimiter.com/docs/configuration): the state directory, the configuration file, the cache, and the agent settings.
- [CLI reference](https://openlimiter.com/docs/cli): every command, with its flags, its output and its exit codes.
- [Security and privacy](https://openlimiter.com/docs/security): what is guaranteed, what is deliberately not done, and how to report a problem.
- [Roadmap](https://openlimiter.com/docs/roadmap): what is planned and not yet built.
